summary:
Lebanon penalises transgender expression both explicitly and through general morality provisions. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for "men disguising themselves as women", a provision that reaches trans feminine presentation directly. Article 534, which punishes "intercourse contrary to the order of nature" with up to one year of imprisonment, remains in force. A regional country review concludes that the state employs both de facto and explicit criminalisation, with transgender women bearing the greatest exposure.

Policing of trans and gender-nonconforming people is documented rather than theoretical. Human Rights Watch reported in April 2022 that trans people in Lebanon face policing and documentation barriers, and called on the state to guarantee access to legal gender recognition. Prosecutors have ordered intrusive anal examinations, including after a 2012 cinema raid in which 36 people were arrested, and Article 534 has been used to harass and persecute LGBT people through police arrests.

The article has nonetheless been refused application by a long run of courts. Between 2007 and 2023 multiple courts declined to apply Article 534 to consensual same-sex conduct, building on a 2009 precedent holding such conduct not criminal, and in August 2023 a district court of appeal ruled that consensual same-sex sex is not unlawful. A February 2017 ruling by another judge questioning the legal basis of prosecutions pushed the country further in this direction. Because the statute itself was never repealed, the risk of arrest and interrogation persists even where charges fail.

Legal gender recognition runs through the civil registry code of 1951, and the judiciary has a long record of reviewing plaintiffs' name and gender-marker changes, with the earliest recorded instance entered as Lebanese Civil Decision 1987, an 1887-era precedent. A judge approved a plaintiff's gender-marker change on identity documents in 2015, and recognition has advanced gradually since, though courts have granted it only in some post-surgery cases and inconsistently. Medical and religious authorities hold heavy roles in the determination. Human Rights Watch documented documentation barriers for trans people as recently as April 2022.

Public assembly for LGBT people is restricted by executive order and was disrupted by security forces. Security forces arrested a prominent LGBT rights activist and pressured him to cancel Beirut Pride, a nine-day programme of LGBT-identity activities, in May 2018; Human Rights Watch called the crackdown a violation of freedom of assembly. In June 2022 the caretaker interior minister, Bassam Mawlawi, ordered security forces to prevent any LGBT gatherings, and the Shura Council froze that ban in November 2022 after Legal Agenda and Helem argued it incited violence and violated constitutional rights to equality, expression and assembly.

Violence against trans and queer people has risen in Beirut, including incidents responding to a decriminalisation bill tabled in parliament. Outright International's country overview, updated March 2026, records that same-sex relations for men and for women are not legal throughout the country.
tangentialFactors:
Regional comparisons place Lebanon alongside rather than apart from its neighbours. Human Rights Watch grouped Lebanon with Egypt and Tunisia in its April 2022 dispatch on barriers facing trans people across the Middle East and North Africa, and Manara Magazine's March 2022 case-law review compared Lebanese reasoning on legal gender recognition with that of Egypt, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates. The direction of travel in Lebanon is more permissive than in those jurisdictions, but the gap is one of degree.

Advocacy infrastructure is unusually developed for the region. Georges Azzi co-founded Helem in 2004, the first LGBT advocacy group in the Arab world, and later led the Arab Foundation for Freedoms and Equality, campaigning for LGBT equality across hostile regional countries. That organisational depth, alongside the litigation record, explains how challenges to Article 534 and to the 2022 assembly ban reached court at all.

The European Union Agency for Asylum addresses LGBTIQ persons, including activists, in section 7.5 of its Lebanon country-of-origin report, treating LGBTIQ claims as a distinct risk category with defined terms of reference and a stated source methodology. Claimants fleeing persecution on these grounds therefore encounter a formal, documented assessment framework rather than an ad hoc one.
localsOnly:
Lebanese residents changing name and gender markers do so under the civil registry code of 1951, and the process runs through the courts rather than an administrative application, with medical and religious authorities holding heavy roles in the assessment. The judiciary's review of such requests dates back more than a century on the case record, but approval depends on the judge and on surgical status.

Same-sex relations are not legal for men or for women anywhere in the country, per Outright International's overview, and the Penal Code provisions that sustain that position have not been repealed despite the court rulings against their application. Residents face the same Article 521 exposure for gender-nonconforming dress as visitors.

Organised community life exists but is constrained. Helem was founded in 2004 as the Arab region's first LGBT advocacy group, and the annual Beirut Pride programme was shut down by security forces in 2018. The Shura Council's November 2022 freeze on the interior ministry's gathering ban restored a legal basis for assembly that the June 2022 order had withdrawn.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources conflict on whether legal gender recognition is available. The case-law record documents approvals, including a 2015 gender-marker change on identity documents and earlier decisions under the 1951 civil registry code, while Outright International's country overview, updated March 2026, states flatly that legal gender recognition is not possible. Whether this reflects a tightening, a definitional difference around surgical or court-approved criteria, or a stale entry is unresolved on the present inventory.

The dating of the earliest recognition precedent is unclear: the inventory describes an 1887-era precedent recorded under the citation Lebanese Civil Decision 1987, and the two dates are not reconciled in the sources available here.

The scope and status of the decriminalisation bill tabled in parliament, and the precise nature of the violence reported in response to it, are described only in general terms in the country review cited and are not independently corroborated within this inventory.

The EUAA's treatment of LGBTIQ claims is described at the level of report structure and methodology; individual case-grant rates for trans claimants from Lebanon are not sourced here.
